gi1_phrase.topic: The phrase Eretz Yisrael HaShlema, the biblical border texts and their readings, and the Aug 2025 remark that put the phrase in the news

claims.text: Greater Israel is an expression with several biblical and political meanings over time; Hebrew Eretz Yisrael HaShlema, 'the Whole (complete) Land of Israel' (shalem = complete), per Greenberg, NYT 1998.
Pipes (1994) argues 'Greater Israel' is an inexact translation of Eretz Yisrael Hashlemah and that the English 'implies a geographical expansion not present in the original'.
Genesis 15:18: covenant with Abram, 'Unto thy seed have I given this land, from the river of Egypt unto the great river, the river Euphrates' (KJV); NIV renders 'from the Wadi of Egypt'.
Deuteronomy 11:24: 'Every place whereon the soles of your feet shall tread shall be yours: from the wilderness and Lebanon, from the river, the river Euphrates, even unto the uttermost sea' (KJV).

Numbers 34:1-15 and Ezekiel 47:13-20 describe a narrower area west of the Jordan divided among the tribes; Ezekiel 47:18 makes the Jordan the eastern boundary; Genesis 15:18-21 promises land to all Abram's offspring including Ishmael.
Gen 15:18 uses nahar ('river'), applied by Hebrews to the largest rivers; the Encyclopedia of The Bible reads it as the Nile (Pelusiac branch) and says there is no textual support to emend to nahal.
The 'Brook of Egypt' (nahal, a seasonal stream bed) of Num 34:5, Josh 15:4, 1 Kings 8:65 and Ezek 47:19 is 'highly probably' the Wadi el-Arish, midway between the Suez Canal and Gaza.
Smith's Bible Dictionary gives two senses for the river of Egypt (the Nile at Gen 15:18; the Wadi el-Arish); the Topical Encyclopedia says it is traditionally identified with Wadi el-Arish.

Pipes argues the river of Egypt likely means Wadi al-Arish (citing Rashi), that Numbers 34 and Ezekiel 47 override the general Genesis wording, and that the covenant includes Ishmael's descendants; he calls the Nile-to-Euphrates idea 'groundless fantasy' and reports it as conventional wisdom in Arab countries and Iran, repeated by Arafat, Nasser, Qadhdhafi, Asad, Rafsanjani.

Pipes: Herzl 'planned to ask the Ottoman sultan' (1898 diary, Zionistisches Tagebuecher vol. 2 p. 650) for land from the Egyptian frontier to the Euphrates but 'did not in fact request' it from anyone.

In an i24NEWS interview aired Tuesday [12] August 2025, asked by Sharon Gal whether he felt connected to the 'Greater Israel' vision, Netanyahu said 'Very much'; he said 'absolutely' when asked if he subscribed to it; he described a 'historic and spiritual mission'.

Al Jazeera did not attribute a territorial list to Netanyahu; it said the concept is 'understood to refer to' the West Bank, Gaza and parts of Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Jordan; The New Arab gave a list in its own voice without source; no Israeli government clarification was reported.

31 Arab and Islamic countries plus the Arab League, OIC and GCC secretaries-general condemned the remarks 'in the strongest terms' as a direct threat to Arab national security; Jordan's foreign ministry called them a 'dangerous and provocative escalation'.
At a cabinet meeting in September 2008 PM Ehud Olmert said 'the notion of Greater Israel no longer exists, and anyone who still believes in it is deluding themselves'.

gi1_versions.topic: Three versions of Greater Israel (maximal, Revisionist, post-1967), named carriers of each, and the currents that rejected territorial maximalism

claims.text: Jabotinsky wrote 'The East Bank of the Jordan' in 1929 (first version to the Yardeniya union, Kaunas, 18 Nov 1929; published Do'ar HaYom 11 Apr 1930); its refrain says both banks of the Jordan belong to the Jewish people; it became one of Betar's best-known songs.

Early Revisionist groups such as Betar and the Irgun regarded the Mandate territory including Transjordan as Greater Israel (citing Pappé); Labor Zionists accepted partition while Revisionists sought Eretz Yisrael HaShlema (Greenberg, NYT).

The Movement for Greater Israel (HaTnu'a Lema'an Eretz Yisrael HaShlema) was formed in July 1967 and called on the government to keep the captured areas and settle them; founders included Labor-movement figures Yitzhak Tabenkin, Nathan Alterman, Haim Gouri, Rachel Yanait Ben-Zvi, Zivia Lubetkin and Yitzhak Zuckerman alongside Uri Zvi Greenberg, Israel Eldad, Shmuel Katz, S.Y. Agnon, Isser Harel and Avraham Yoffe.
The movement's List for the Land of Israel won 7,561 votes (0.6%) in 1969 and no seat; it joined Likud in 1973 (Avraham Yoffe took its seat); in 1976 it merged into La'am within Likud.

The 1977 Likud platform: 'The right of the Jewish people to the land of Israel is eternal and indisputable'; 'Judea and Samaria will not be handed to any foreign administration; between the Sea and the Jordan there will only be Israeli sovereignty'; it opposes any plan that 'relinquishes parts of western Eretz Israel'; settlement 'in all parts of the Land of Israel'.
Begin, elected 1977, did not annex the West Bank and Gaza after taking office (Greenberg, NYT); in the 2000s annexation was part of Likud's platform per Wikipedia.

Shelef: in 1925 a minority of Religious Zionist groups backed a Nile-to-Euphrates homeland; by 2005 the claims had changed to present-day Israel, the Golan, Gaza and the West Bank; the change 'is not yet finished, nor is it irreversible'; the Hardal wing has revived the larger claim.
The guidelines of Israel's 37th government (28 Dec 2022) state: 'The Jewish people has an exclusive and inalienable right to all parts of the Land of Israel'.

The Territorialist Jewish Organization was founded in Basle in July 1905 under Israel Zangwill after the Congress rejected the Uganda programme; it sought land in Africa, Asia and Australia and dissolved in 1925.
Israel's handover of Sinai ended on 25 April 1982 under the Camp David agreements; Yamit was evacuated and levelled; Sharon: 'In Sinai, in Yamit, we have reached the red line of our concessions.'
